To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
beak removal and genetic selection for family performance reduced mortality from beak-inflicting injuries and increased hen-housed egg mass in White Leghorn chickens.
selection for family performance in multiple-hen cage rearing decreased mortality due to cannibalistic pecks and increased hen-housed egg mass.
selection of stocks on family performance in multiple hen cages and beak trimming to one half of the beak's original length reduced mortality from cannibalism and increased hen-housed egg mass.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of selection on cannibalism and short-term production in White Leghorns.
the effects of beak trimming, genetic selection, and their interaction on behavior and production traits in pullets.
the genetic basis for the behavioral and production traits of interest.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
beak-trim treatments had a greater effect on behavior, cannibalsm, and production than genetic selection.
the genetic stock differences were small in magnitude and not of economic importance in comparison to the effects of beak trimming.
selection of White Leghorn stocks on family performance in multiple-hen cage environments has resulted in stocks with reduced cannibalism and improved production traits in multiple-hen environments.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
beak-trim treatments had no effect on behavior, fearfulness, or production in pullets selected for performance.

selection of pullets from the same genetic stock as the parents of the breeder flock resulted in earlier sexual maturity and greater hen-housetype production and egg mass but did not reduce the incidence of cannibalism or the mortality resulting from beak pecking.
selection on family performance in a multiple-hen environment and beak removal reduced the frequency of cannibalistic pecks and increased hen-housed production.

the effects of beak-trimming and selection on cannibalism and egg production are not independent.
the effects of beak trimming on behavior and performance traits were small, but that beak trimming did reduce cannibalism.
beak trimming can have a positive impact on hen-housed egg output and egg quality traits.
